articles.title: Ashwini Vaishnaw cautions industry about cyberattacks, disruption targeting India's growing chip might
articles.text:
Ashwini Vaishnaw cautions industry about cyberattacks, disruption targeting India's growing chip might
The minister for electronics and IT said he has cautioned the industry to keep a constant vigil as India is now emerging as a country that has the capability to design and manufacture chips.
India's growing semiconductor heft could be seen as a "threat" by established interests in the global chip value chain, and the industry must guard against cyberattacks and other disruptions from those opposed to the country's rise, Minister for Electronics and IT, Ashwini Vaishnaw, has said.
In an interview to PTI, Vaishnaw said he has cautioned the industry in clear terms to keep a constant vigil as India is now emerging as a country that has the capability to design and manufacture chips, a position that will "obviously" be seen as a threat by many other established interests.
"We have to continuously be watchful of the potential geopolitical risks which will arise because India is now emerging as a country which can design and manufacture chips. Obviously that will be seen as a threat by many other established players," he said.
As many countries look to India as a trusted partner and develop and manufacture their products here, the minister said India cannot afford to take its position lightly and must stay vigilant.
"But we should not take it lightly. We should be cognizant of the risks and challenges which will come from other players. So I have very candidly told the entire industry that be prepared for cyber attacks, be prepared for any other kinds of threats and any other kinds of disruptions that might get created by the countries who don't like India to come up in the semiconductor value chain," he said.
The minister said that since his frank and candid discussion on the issue, the industry is now cognizant and "they would certainly take the right measures".
India is seeking to build a larger presence in the global semiconductor value chain, making the sector increasingly important to the country's technology and manufacturing ambitions. The government has also sought to expand the ecosystem beyond chip assembly and testing to include design, equipment, materials and fabrication.
The Union Cabinet in July approved Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of Rs 1,27,500 crore, to support chip design, semiconductor equipment and materials, fabs, advanced packaging, research and development and talent development.
The programme builds on the momentum of the first phase, under which 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects with investments of more than Rs 1.64 lakh crore have been approved. Five, including Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi, are already in commercial production.
India's chip push marks a bold attempt to move beyond packaging and build a broader domestic supply chain, while attracting global companies to manufacture and develop semiconductor technologies in India.
The government recently said it had received about Rs 1 lakh crore in investment commitments under the second phase of the semiconductor scheme.
Investor interest was in full focus at the just-concluded SEMICON India event, a mega showcase of the nation's chip-making heft, that saw a slew of big-ticket announcements, including Applied Materials' USD 5 billion India plan through 2035, Lam Research's proposed Rs 10,000-crore investment, Tata Electronics' 363-acre vendor park at Dholera and Fujifilm's Rs 800-crore semiconductor materials plant.

articles.title: ¿Quieres hacer más repeticiones en el gimnasio? Llévate una barrita de chocolate, pero no te la comas
articles.text:
Se habla mucho de la creatina para tener más energía y poder hacer más repeticiones durante el ejercicio físico. ¿Pero y si ese mismo efecto se consiguiese con algo tan simple como oler chocolate? Según un estudio realizado recientemente por científicos de la Universidad Malaya, podría ser una buena opción, tanto con chocolate negro como con chocolate con leche. Eso sí, los motivos por lo se consiguen con uno y otro parecen ser diferentes.
Chocolate negro, con leche o agua. Para llevar a cabo este estudio, una serie de voluntarios tuvieron que practicar el ejercicio de extensión de piernas, en el que se levanta un peso apoyado sobre las espinillas a la vez que se estiran las extremidades inferiores. Todos ellos estaban moderadamente entrenados y tuvieron que hacer 10 horas de ayuno antes de participar en el experimento. Una vez llegado el momento del ejercicio, lo hicieron pasando aleatoriamente por tres fases: chocolate negro (90% cacao), chocolate con leche (60% cacao) y agua. Antes del ejercicio y entre series tuvieron que oler un líquido que en una tanda fue chocolate negro, en otra chocolate con leche y en otra agua. Es decir, todos los voluntarios participaron en todos los supuestos en un orden aleatorio. Además, tanto antes como después contestaron unas preguntas sobre sus niveles de hambre.
Saciedad y repeticiones. Cuando olieron agua fue cuando menos repeticiones lograron del ejercicio. Por su parte, al oler chocolate negro hicieron una media de 18 repeticiones más y con el chocolate con leche un promedio de 9 repeticiones extra en la extensión de piernas. Cuando se les preguntó por sus niveles de saciedad o la percepción del olor, quienes olieron el chocolate negro refirieron sentirse más saciados, aunque el olor no les pareciera especialmente agradable. Los que olieron el chocolate con leche no se sintieron saciados, pero sí señalaron que les gustó mucho el olor.
Las causas. Los motivos por los que se dieron estos resultados no están claros, aunque los autores del estudio creen que se debe a que nuestro cerebro conecta los olores de alimentos conocidos y agradables con distintos mecanismos beneficiosos para el ejercicio. Por ejemplo, el chocolate negro genera sensación de saciedad en el cerebo, de modo que se engaña al sistema digestivo para que nos sintamos llenos y con energía suficiente para poder hacer unas cuantas repeticiones de fuerza más. En cambio, el chocolate con leche actúa a través de regiones vinculadas a las emociones. Al tratarse de un aroma tan agradable, los participantes se sentían mejor y más motivados para hacer ejercicio pensando en la recompensa que podría llegar después.
Hay bastantes limitaciones. En este estudio hay varios datos que nos hacen tomar los resultados con cautela. El primero es que se realizó solo con 23 hombres jóvenes, sanos y moderadamente entrenados, por lo que se trata de una muestra pequeña y muy poco diversa. Sería interesante repetir el estudio con una mayor variedad de participantes y, por supuesto, muchas más personas.
Por otro lado, los resultados de un estudio son mucho más fiables cuando las personas del grupo control no saben que lo son. En este caso, el grupo control, ese en el que no se esperaban cambios, es el que olió agua. Al tratarse de un líquido transparente e inodoro, podían ser conscientes de estar tomando una especie de placebo y, por lo tanto, experimentar cierta sugestión. Finalmente, cabe destacar que no se ha hecho un análisis del cerebro ni los niveles de hormonas, por lo que es imposible saber si los resultados son casuales o si realmente existe esa explicación biológica que los autores han intuido.
Sigue tomando creatina si te gusta y te va bien. La creatina nos aporta muchos beneficios más allá de permitirnos unas cuantas repeticiones más. De hecho, en el estudio no se habla de ella en ningún momento. Simplemente, es un ejemplo para que veamos que, a veces, un resultado se puede obtener por las vías más inesperadas. De todos modos, tampoco pierdes nada por oler algo de chocolate entre series. Quizás te conviertas en el bicho raro del gimnasio, pero también puedes empezar con una tendencia que ayude a aportar más datos a la ciencia.

articles.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets | TechCrunch
articles.text:
This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale.
At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence, so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems.
But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.”
To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities.
That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me.
Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out?
No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic.
In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building.
Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario: If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention.
This post was first published on September 18, 2026.

articles.title: Este delfín ha encontrado una forma bastante repugnante de conseguir comida: hacer vomitar a sus presas
articles.text:
Los delfines han sido vistos por muchos como seres marinos realmente pacíficos y muy adorables, pero la realidad es que cuentan con diferentes técnicas que no cumplen con esta idealización. Y uno de ellos, la verdad, es que ha sorprendido, sobre todo por lo original que es a la hora de cazar una presa para comérsela.
El método de 'Bubbles'. La investigación que ha acaparado un gran protagonismo ha surgido este mismo mes de septiembre a través de la revista Ecology and Evolution. Aquí los investigadores hicieron un seguimiento de la fauna marina y centraron su atención en un macho de delfín mular apodado como 'Bubbles'.
El objetivo aquí era ver exactamente cómo vivían y se alimentaban, y aquí observaron que en un gran número de ocasiones el delfín perseguía a un pez conocido como carángido ojón. Pero lo más interesante es que, durante las persecuciones que mantenía, el delfín esperaba a que el pez terminara vomitando todo lo que tenía en su estómago para, posteriormente, tragarse este residuo que había sido expulsado. Y encima seleccionaba a cada uno de los peces que iba a perseguir de entre un gran banco.
Y tiene lógica porque este comportamiento es perfectamente compatible con lo que en zoología se denomina 'cleptoparasitismo', es decir, una práctica de obtener alimento que ha sido producido, capturado o ingerido previamente por otro animal. Aunque en este caso no es que el delfín esté robando una presa que el pez lleve en la boca para él, sino que aprovecha el alimento que el pez se ha tomado y digerido para tomárselo él tras obligarle a vomitar en la huida.
Cómo lo saben. Tiene bastante mérito conocer exactamente cuál es la mejor presa porque tiene que haber tenido algo en el estómago de provecho para posteriormente comer. Y aquí los investigadores creen que la ecolocalización durante la fase de selección de presa es crucial, porque aparte de ser usada para diferenciar entre las especies de los peces, también podría ser interesante para conocer la estructura y la forma de estos.
Aunque todavía queda mucho por saber por delante, puesto que estamos hablando de que es un comportamiento que se ha visto en un único delfín de la región y es por ello que queda mucha investigación por delante. Pero el problema que vemos aquí es que es sumamente complicado encontrar este tipo de casos y captarlos por parte de los investigadores. Aunque aquí la tecnología podría abrir una puerta fascinante a ver un poco más de cerca cómo el delfín se comporta en su medio natural.

articles.title: I tested the LaserPecker LX2, and small businesses will love this laser cutter
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The LX2 is an impressive fully enclosed machine offering a generous 500 x 305mm work area, modular heads, and plenty of accessories. The 40W powered through 20mm basswood with a clean cut. However, the software is still in Beta, and you need to put in a little more work than some other machines of this type; still, it's a great machine for any small business.
Pros
- +Ideally sized and specced for small businesses
- +Fast engraving and cutting speeds
- +Tool-free laser module swapping
- +Large, fully enclosed workspace
Cons
- -Needs some experimentation with settings
- -Only four base slats supplied
- -Air Assist and data lines not integrated into the module
Why you can trust TechRadar
LaserPecker has been in the laser engraving and cutting sector for a while. Still, the LX2 is its first fully enclosed system of this type, and the first that feels genuinely suited to home and small-business use rather than a workshop with proper ventilation and space to spare.
The LX2 pairs the safety of a full enclosure with a modular head system, swapping between 20W, 40W, and 60W diode and 2W infrared without tools, enabling this machine to cover a far wider range of materials and objects than a fixed single-laser engraver. However, those machines are now becoming scarce.
In this test, I’ve looked at the LX2 with the 40W diode and 2W IR heads, connected directly to a MacBook Pro M1 Max, running LaserPecker Design Space in Beta, since the full release does not yet support the LX2.
LaserPecker LX2: Price & availability
The LaserPecker LX2 is available direct from the manufacturer in the US here, and in the UK here.
At time of review, prices start at $1599 (down from $1999) / £1349 (down from £1799) for the 20W standard bundle. The 40W Standard Bundle is $1799 / £1849.
LaserPecker LX2: Design
Laser technology: Interchangeable diode and IR laser modules
Build area: 500 x 305mm
Dimensions: 779.5 x 609.2 x 281.15mm
Weight: 22.5kg, main unit
Bed: Slatted support base, four slats supplied as standard
Software: LaserPecker Design Space (Beta, required for LX2 support), LightBurn also supported
Materials: Wood, acrylic and, with the 2W IR head, metals and plastics; see 
Laser options: 20W diode, 40W diode (tested), 2W 1064nm IR (tested), 60W support 
Camera: 12MP / 6K positioning camera
Connectivity: USB, Wi-Fi; USB-C on the LX2 end, USB-A on the computer end; a Mac needs an adapter
Standard accessories: Smart Air Assist, cutting slats, fire extinguisher port
The LX2 is relatively heavy at 22.5kg, but despite its size, it is well built and easy enough to lift and move around in the workshop; it’s also lighter than the two other cutters I already have, and at 779.5 x 609.2 x 281.15mm in size, a standard, properly braced project desk is more than sufficient to hold it.
Like most fully enclosed machines, it has a lift-over top lid that lets you watch the cut or engraving in progress, and a handy front-panel opening that makes loading material easier and lets you use the LX2 as a front-loader if you don't have headroom above the machine. It is the only machine I have come across with this feature.
Round the back are all the ports and connectors, including the USB-C that connects to your computer, with both Mac and PC supported. One oddity worth knowing: the USB-C end of the cable goes into the LX2, and the USB-A end into your computer, so a Mac needs an adapter.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Alongside that are a USB-A port for a USB key, a security key port (which needs a key installed for the machine to run at all), the fire extinguisher port, Air Assist, and the smoke outlet.
The Air Assist itself is a surprise. It’s still external to the device, and while it is nicely designed, it sits alongside the machine rather than being integrated. It connects via its own cable, similar to USB-C but with a proprietary fit, and I found the connector rather delicate; a second cable was needed to complete the test after the original broke.
Inside is the 500 x 305mm work area, with markings on the base for camera alignment during calibration and each cut. There are also two cameras, with a live preview back to the software; accurate positioning is easy enough, as you’d expect on this level of machine.
Once again, there is no honeycomb grid included, something that is an increasingly common omission, and LaserPecker supplies only four thin slats to support material. Four is not enough. If you buy this machine, budget for at least four more, since without them you will be constantly repositioning the slats you have to support each new piece of material.
Otherwise, the design is aesthetically stunning, and the build quality is superb. There’s no doubt that this is a solid machine, but even on initial unboxing you can see a few areas that need a little more design attention.
LaserPecker LX2: Features
The feature list mirrors most other fully enclosed laser cutters at this price, and the build quality was obvious as soon as I lifted the machine out of its packaging. If the cutting accuracy holds up, this looks like a great option for a small business, and the modular heads add the flexibility to work across a huge range of materials and objects rather than being locked to one laser type.
The design is aesthetically stunning, and looks good on the workshop bench. The machine is big, but so is the work area it buys you. I like that it has front- and top-loading capabilities.
One of the big features is the ability to fit different modules with three diode options: 20W, 40W and 60W and a 2W IR for metal. This offers one of the most flexible solutions out there, so if you are running a business, this will be a great option.
Fitting a module is simple enough, though it does mean connecting a data cable and an air assist tube each time. I would still prefer these integrated into the head itself, but it is easy enough as it stands.
Once running, the engraving and cutting offer impressive speeds, and speed is one of the LX2’s headline features: 1,000mm/s with acceleration up to 10,000mm/s² which means that if used with some of the larger accessories, such as the optional conveyor, much larger projects can be tackled.
Finally, and this is one of the lead features, there are two internal positioning cameras that help with placement accuracy in the software; this positioning accuracy is essential when working with the 2W IR head, where the finished mark is harder to preview by eye.
LaserPecker LX2: Performance
Setup, calibration and connecting the software took around an hour in total, roughly half an hour unpacking and fitting the head, and another half hour on calibration and getting connected. That is in line with other enclosed engravers of this type I have looked at recently.
Fitting the head was easy enough, if not quite as smooth as some rivals, and plugging in the data cable and Air Assist tube alongside it was straightforward, though I would still rather see it integrated into the head itself. Running the vent to an external filter is worth doing and worth budgeting for, though LaserPecker has not yet listed a price.
Installing the software meant finding the Beta build specifically, since the standard release of LaserPecker Design Space does not yet support the LX2. The first run takes you through mandatory safety training before you can use the machine, then through a USB connection to start with. Calibration is more convoluted than rivals I have used.
LaserPecker Design Space is all well laid out, although there are sections where you can still see that this software is in Beta, such as the WiFi connection, re-running calibration and some stability issues. However, it’s extensive, and once you start to familiarise yourself with how it works, it does generally make sense.
Importing designs requires you to add SVG files as an example project and then open them, but line and fill information is retained and accessing those settings and adjusting power and speed is straight forwrad. I also liked the fact that there is a set of material presets, and the settings for these are close to spot on.
When you first get started with a material there is a test chart installed which will show you the effect at the different powers and speeds, this is well worth running on any new material so that you can fine tune the settings.
Some experimentation is still needed to get the perfect result for a given material and finish, but this is a starting point rather than a blank slate for every job, and it improved noticeably over a couple of weeks of regular use.
One issue that I did have during testing was with the Air Assist or to be more accurate the proprietary cable that looks very much like USB-C, and the one I received was delicate enough that the connector broke partway through the test.
That is why some of the wood samples from this review show scorching; results from earlier in testing, before the cable failed, are noticeably cleaner. Worth knowing if you are relying on Air Assist for consistent results.
Cutting 20mm basswood with multiple passes, with Air Assist working and the settings properly dialled in, produced results with little charring or residue, though getting there took time and experimentation rather than being right first time.
The 2W IR head fitted just as easily as the 40W diode, and its results were excellent; again, with no ready-made preset for every material, building the right settings is part of the process, and this is perfectly normal.
Testing the 40W module, it was able to produce clean and substantial cuts, and I tended to measure the material distance prior to each cut just to ensure the best performance.
LaserPecker LX2: Final verdict
The LX2 is a great machine with a few rough edges and odd decisions. Looking at the negatives, the first has to be the air assist cable to the machine; this is needed for automatic operation.
In the review I ended up just running a power cable directly to the Air Assist and bypassing the auto features. While breaking the cable partway through it was good to see that the Air Assist could be powered in a different way.
In use, the large workspace, high speed when needed, camera alignment and clean cuts definitely make this an appealing machine, but the software at present does hold it back; there are just small issues that need ironing out, such as the calibration process, the loading of files and some stability.
If you’re a serious maker or small business producing a genuine mix of cut wood, engraved products and customised metal items, where the modular approach makes sense at this price and with the flexibility of all those accessories, all makes this look like a great small business solution.
Should you buy the LaserPecker LX2
| Value: | Well-balanced price, with huge creative potential | 4 | 
| Design: | Large and fully enclosed with large work area | 4.5 | 
| Features | Modular lasers and availability of plenty of accessories future-proof the design | 4 | 
| Performance | Fast cutting, precise, detailed engraving, but some software issues hold it back | 4 | 
| Total | A great machine with a few small issues; if you’re aware, it will provide excellent service. | 4 | 
Buy it if...
You're running a small business.
You regularly produce personalised products and need a fast, enclosed machine with enough workspace to handle efficient batch production.
You want maximum versatility.
Swappable diode and infrared modules let one machine tackle cutting, engraving and detailed metal marking across many different materials.
Don't buy it if...
You're into occasional light engraving.
If you only engrave coasters or small gifts occasionally, cheaper compact machines can provide sufficient capability for considerably less money.
You have limited workshop space.
The large footprint and 22.5kg weight mean the LX2 really needs a permanent, sturdy workbench rather than occasional desk space.
For more crafting tech, I've tested and reviewed all the best 3D printers and the best laser engravers.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.

articles.title: Dell Pro 7 Webcam 4K Review: Sounds surprisingly great
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Dell Pro 7 is a compact 4K / 60 fps webcam that will make you look pretty good and sound even better, but it has a lot of competition.
Pros
- +Good image quality in perfect lighting
- +Surprisingly good mic
- +Windows Hello compatible, presence detection
Cons
- -Auto color balancing was off
- -Software doesn't offer much in the way of adjustments
- -Below average performance in poor lighting conditions
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
The best webcams are getting smaller, cheaper, and faster, apparently — Dell's newest premium webcam is a 4K webcam that streams video at a maximum resolution of 4K / 60fps, which is definitely a faster and smoother frame rate than your typical Dell webcam buyer needs. There's not much you can really do with those numbers if you're not a content creator — and especially not in a professional setting, as most video conferencing apps limit your outgoing stream to 1080p or lower.
Luckily, the Dell Pro 7 has more than just smooth, high-res video going for it — it also features Windows Hello compatibility, presence detection, smart image enhancements, and built-in dual beam-forming mics that might be the first built-in webcam mics we can actually recommend. At $199.99, it's priced right alongside 4K webcams such as the Logitech MX Brio and the Insta360 Link 2 4K, which means it has some pretty tough competition.
Design
The Dell Pro 7 webcam is a 4K / 60fps webcam with a solid, sturdy fabric-covered chassis and a glass lens cover. It features a large Sony STARVIS CMOS sensor, an auto-focus lens, 4x digital zoom, and it has a maximum aperture of f/2.0. It has a built-in physical privacy shutter and comes with a detachable USB-C cable and monitor mount.
The Dell Pro 7 is similar in design to the cheaper Dell Pro 5 Webcam 2K — it features the same low-profile oval-shaped body, though the Dell Pro 7 is quite a bit larger and heavier than the Dell Pro 5. The Dell Pro 7 measures approximately 2.6 inches (66mm) deep by 2.1 inches (53.3mm) wide, and is about 1.4 inches (35.6mm) tall. This is the same height as the Dell Pro 5, though the Dell Pro 7 is both deeper and wider than its cheaper sibling. It's also heavier — Dell lists its weight at 8.48 ounces (240.4g), but that includes the mount. However the webcam alone still weighs around 3.46 ounces (98g). By comparison, the Dell Pro 5 weighs 7.41 ounces (210g) including its mount, and weighs 2.57 ounces (73g) without it (but including the cable, which is not detachable).
It is heavier than the Dell Pro 5, but it's not unusually heavy for a premium 4K webcam. The Razer Kiyo Pro Ultra, for example, weighs about 6.28 ounces (178g) alone, and that jumps up to 11.89 ounces (337.08g) when you include the mount. The Logitech MX Brio weighs just 4.83 ounces (137g) alone, but it weighs 11.04 ounces (313g) with its mount. And the Dell Pro 7 is also quite a bit smaller than its competition — I especially like how relatively low-profile it is at 1.4 inches, which is less than half the height of the 3.01-inch (76.5mm) height of the Kiyo Pro Ultra.
The Dell Pro 7 has a built-in physical shutter that you can close with a switch on top of the webcam. It looks just like the built-in physical privacy shutter on the Dell Pro 5, but it has a built-in spring-loaded mechanism so it snaps into place when you slide the switch. (The Dell Pro 5 doesn't have this mechanism — you need to manually slide it all the way.) The spring-loaded mechanism definitely made it feel more premium than the Dell Pro 5, but it still needed to be pressed fairly hard to activate, which means you can't really use the shutter without messing up your frame.
The Dell Pro 7 comes with a detachable monitor mount that attaches to the webcam via magnet. The mount is a pretty standard clamp-style monitor mount, with a lip at the front that hooks over your monitor and a rubber-coated adjustable "foot" that sits against the back of your monitor to stabilize the setup. The mount attaches to the Dell Pro 7 via a relatively stable magnetic attachment point, and the camera can tilt (approximately 90 degrees forward) and swivel while mounted. On the bottom of the webcam you'll also find a universal tripod attachment mounting point so you can use it with a tripod or a different, third-party mount. The mount itself does not have a tripod attachment point, which is a little disappointing as it means you'll be limited to the movement options of whatever third-party mount/tripod you're using.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The mount is hefty and stable, weighing about 4.83 ounces (137g). It's basically the exact same mount that comes with the Dell Pro 5, though it has a slightly textured rubber coating on its "foot," while the Dell Pro 5's mount features soft, smooth rubber. The weight and quality feel much more consistent with the build of the Dell Pro 7, however.
In the box, the Dell Pro 7 comes with a 6.5-foot (2m) heavy-duty USB-C to USB-C cable (USB 3.0) with a built-in USB-C to USB-A converter, the detachable monitor mount, and the webcam itself. The cable is definitely very thick and sturdy — a little too thick and sturdy, as bumping it kept displacing the webcam. The built-in USB-C to USB-A adapter is a nice touch, though you will still need to plug it into a USB 3.0 port if you want to get the full 4K picture quality and use some of the "smart" features (such as the "smart" HDR).
Specs
| Resolution FPS | 4K / 30, 60fps; 1080p / 30, 60fps; 720p / 30, 60fps | 
| Diagonal Field of View | 90 degrees | 
| Zoom | 4x digital zoom | 
| Autofocus | Yes | 
| HDR | Yes | 
| Microphone | Dual beam-forming mics | 
| Connection | Wired (USB 3.0) | 
| Mount | Universal clip | 
| Dimensions | 2.6 x 2.1 x 1.4 inches / 66 x 53.3 x 35.6mm | 
| Weight | 8.48oz / 240.4g (including mount) | 
| Software | Dell | 
| Special Features | Windows Hello, AI | 
| MSRP / Price at Time of Review | $199.99 | 
| Release Date | June 11, 2026 | 
Well-lit Performance
The Dell Pro 7 is a 4K webcam that records video in 4K, 1080p, and 720p resolution at both 60 and 30fps — which makes it somewhat rare, as most 4K webcams record a maximum of 4K / 30fps. Not that this matters for most users, as streaming and video chat platforms still generally limit outgoing streams to 1080p at most. Still, I guess it's worth noting if you're looking for a webcam that you can use to record action sequences on.
We started out by testing the Dell Pro 7's performance in what is basically an "ideal" (and very unrealistic) webcam lighting scenario. In this scenario there are two professional lights in front of me (behind my monitor set up): a ring light and a key light. I also have four monitors — three 27-inch monitors and one ultra-wide 34-inch monitor, plus some negligible ambient lighting from various peripherals (including my desk). There are two desk lamps behind me, as well as an arching floor lamp above me. All in all, this is an aggressively well-lit scenario (and a very unlikely one, unless you happen to be a professional content creator).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Dell Pro 7 looked very good in our well-lit scenario. It did a great job of reigning in its auto-exposure in response to the lighting, which is something even the best webcams usually have more trouble with. It managed to keep the scene pretty evenly lit, even as I moved around the room, while also keeping it from looking too evenly lit, i.e., flat and featureless. Its auto white balancing was okay, though it trended toward the cool end of the spectrum. Actually, the colors on this webcam always seemed to be just a little too cool, even with some tweaking in the software. Not the worst thing in the world, but it was frustrating that I couldn't get the color to where I wanted it with adjustments.
That said, while the Dell Pro 7 produced an objectively very good image overall, it didn't really stand out in any way aside from that. I suppose that's not a bad thing, especially for a webcam that's (maybe) slightly more aimed at the workplace, but it mostly made me think of all the other $200 4K webcams you can pick up instead of the Dell Pro 7. Also, while the webcam did a pretty solid job of capturing still photos, the auto-focus was a little slow — which sort of negates the benefit of a 4K / 60 fps capture rate.
Low-Light Performance
To test the webcam's low-light performance, I turned off all of the lights and all of my monitors except for one 27-inch monitor. For consistency, I opened the standard Google home page, which is mostly white, on one half of the monitor and the Windows 11 camera app on the other half. This scenario leaves me in complete darkness save for the light from one 27-inch monitor, which is still quite a bit more light than a laptop user would have if they were sitting in the dark.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Dell Pro 7 performed moderately well in our low-light scenario. It did an okay job of lighting the scene — the picture looked better than most older webcams, but that's about it (and that's not saying much). There was a lot of noise / graininess and artifacting, however, especially when I moved. And the autofocus had (unsurprisingly) even more trouble tracking me in the dark, and an evenly-lit blurry mess is still a blurry mess.
No webcam performs particularly well in low light, because sensor size is a major factor in low-light performance and webcams are... just not that big. But compared to other 4K webcams such as the Elgato Facecam Pro and the Logitech MX Brio, the Dell Pro 7 definitely comes in a little below average.
Overexposed Performance
To test the Dell Pro 7's performance in overexposed lighting scenarios, I turned off all of the lights in front of me and three of my monitors. That left me with my overhead and background lights, as well as one 27-inch monitor. This isn't the most extreme overexposed lighting scenario, but it's a fairly common one as most offices tend to have a lot of overhead lighting (and only professional streamers put bright, studio-grade lighting directly behind a monitor).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Dell Pro 7 performed fairly well in this lighting scenario, though it struggled to find a natural-looking color balance (and it kept veering cooler). This is another scenario in which no webcam does particularly well — for the most part, it's enough to just not get blown out by the lighting behind you. But the Logitech MX Brio, which is probably one of the Dell Pro 7's closest competitors, did a much better job here.
Features and Software
The Dell Pro 7 is configurable via the Dell Display and Peripheral Manager, which lets you adjust camera and picture settings and set up the webcam's various features, such as Windows Hello, presence detection, and the "smart" image enhancements.
While the Dell Display and Peripheral Manager has all the settings and adjustments you might expect in a webcam app, I didn't feel like the various manual adjustments for exposure, saturation, contrast, sharpness, and vibrance were very powerful, which was a bit surprising as usually these settings are too powerful. But this wasn't too much of an issue for me, as the picture is already pretty good — just not perfect — out of the box.
In addition to image enhancements and color adjustments, you can also set up several features in Dell Display and Peripheral Manager — such as face-tracking and auto-framing; "smart" HDR, exposure, and auto white balance; and Windows Hello compatibility. Like the Dell Pro 5, the Dell Pro 7 also has a "document view" feature designed to better focus on and display documents, as well as an "object focus" mode that can be activated using gesture controls (or manually).
The Dell Pro 7 has built-in dual beam-forming microphones, and while a built-in microphone is not really something most people are looking for in a webcam (especially as they generally tend to be terrible), the Dell Pro 7's built-in mics were surprisingly good — and not just for a webcam, but... in general. In fact, this might be the first webcam with a mic I can actually recommend.
The Dell Pro 7's mics picked up my voice very well — it came through loud, clear, and surprisingly vibrant and full, even when I was sitting at a normal distance from the webcam and speaking casually (i.e., not trying to speak "into" the mic). There was a little fuzziness and distortion around the edges of my words, and it picked up the clacking on my keyboard and the clicking on my mouse almost as well as it picked up my voice (and the software-based noise reduction in the app almost immediately started swallowing my words), but as long as you're not trying to type and talk at the same time the Dell Pro 7's mic sounds good. Not as good as a standalone USB gaming mic, of course, but on par with the average gaming headset mic.
Bottom Line
The Dell Pro 7 is actually a pretty solid 4K webcam, if not a particularly thrilling one. While I don't think most people looking at the Dell Pro 7 are going to be fiending for 60fps, I'm sure there are probably at least two people who will appreciate it. For everyone else, the Dell Pro 7 has a nice suite of office-friendly features, including presence detection to lock your PC when you're not sitting in front of it, Windows Hello compatibility for extra security, and things like document view and gesture control and an extra-wide field of view for when you need to run a remote 4K, 60fps meeting with lots of people (and documents).
But if you don't see yourself running speedy, highly-detailed multi-person webcam meetings, the similarly-priced Logitech MX Brio does a better job at making you look good... which is a big part of what webcams are for, right? The Dell Pro 7 outputs a decent picture (in relatively "ideal" lighting), but this webcam is not really about the picture — it's about everything else.
Sarah Jacobsson Purewal is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware covering peripherals, software, and custom builds. You can find more of her work in PCWorld, Macworld, TechHive, CNET, Gizmodo, Tom's Guide, PC Gamer, Men's Health, Men's Fitness, SHAPE, Cosmopolitan, and just about everywhere else.

articles.title: Toyota: Roboter arbeiten bald Seite an Seite mit Menschen
articles.text:
Seite an Seite mit Menschen: Toyota baut 400.000 Roboter für seine Fabriken
Schon jetzt sollen in Japan rund 500.000 Industrieroboter im Einsatz sein. In Deutschland sind es etwa halb so viele. Bald dürfte sich die Zahl der weltweit in Fabriken eingesetzten Roboter deutlich steigern. Denn Toyota, der nach Absatzzahlen größte Automobilkonzern der Welt, hat große Pläne.
400.000 Roboter für Toyota-Fabriken
Wie Nikkei Asia berichtet, will Toyota seine Produktionsstätten modernisieren. In diesem Rahmen sollen künftig 400.000 selbst entwickelte Roboter in den eigenen Fabriken sowie den Fabriken von Konzerntöchtern und Zulieferfirmen eingesetzt werden.
Dabei soll es vor allem um den humanoiden Roboter Eley (Embodied Learning Robot For Enhanced Yield) gehen. Toyota zufolge ist dieser dank KI-Unterstützung darauf ausgelegt, durch physische Interaktion zu lernen und hohe Leistung sowie Produktivität zu erbringen.
Menschenähnliche Struktur, aber keine Beine
Dank seiner menschenähnlichen Körperstruktur, inklusive der entsprechenden Gelenkabstände, der Armdicke und dem Vorhandensein von Schulterblättern, soll Eley menschliche Bewegungen leichter imitieren können. Statt Beine verfügt der Roboter allerdings über eine rollende Plattform, die ihm mehr Stabilität verleihen soll.
Zudem kommen statt fünf nur zwei Finger pro Hand zum Einsatz, die sich zu Greifern zusammenführen lassen. Damit sollen die meisten Tätigkeiten erledigt werden können, wie ingenieur.de schreibt. In Toyota-typischer Manier verzichtet der Konzern bei Eley zudem auf ein Gesicht. Stattdessen gibt es einen funktionalen Bildschirm.
Roboter sollen gemeinsam mit Menschen arbeiten
Geplant ist, dass die humanoiden Roboter Seite an Seite mit Menschen in den Fabriken des Autobauers arbeiten. In den kommenden Jahren will Toyota rund 150.000 der Roboter für die Fertigung in den eigenen Fabriken fitmachen. Weitere 250.000 Roboter sollen bei den schon erwähnten Konzerntöchtern und Zulieferern eingesetzt werden.
Insgesamt soll der Toyota-Konzern für die Modernisierung seiner Werke ab 2028 jährlich rund 6,5 Milliarden Dollar in die Hand nehmen. Das Geld soll in die Renovierung und den Umbau der Fabriken sowie in die Entwicklung und den Einsatz der Roboter in den Fabriken fließen.

articles.title: Apple Watch Series 12 et Ultra 4 : cette fonction santé bien pratique manque à l’appel
articles.text:
Les nouvelles montres connectées d'Apple embarquent un processeur profondément remanié et plusieurs fonctionnalités inédites. Pourtant, une capacité santé vieille de cinq ans ne figure tout simplement plus dans la liste du matériel compatible.
La détection automatique du lavage des mains manque étonnamment à l’appel sur les nouvelles Apple Watch Series 12 et Ultra 4. Une absence d’autant plus surprenante que cette fonction est toujours intégrée à watchOS 27 et qu’Apple continue de la documenter.
Apple Watch : cette fonction née pendant la pandémie est toujours là… sauf sur les derniers modèles
Lancée en 2020 avec watchOS 7, la détection automatique du lavage des mains permet à l’Apple Watch de reconnaître les gestes associés à cette activité et de lancer un minuteur. La fonction a depuis continué son chemin dans l’écosystème d’Apple : elle est toujours présente dans watchOS 27 et dispose encore de sa propre catégorie dans l’application Santé, y compris avec iOS 27.2.
C'est en consultant la documentation officielle consacrée au système que nos confrères de 9to5Mac ont relevé un détail pour le moins surprenant. Les Apple Watch Series 11 et Ultra 3 figurent bel et bien parmi les modèles compatibles, contrairement aux Series 12 et Ultra 4. Pour l’heure, la marque à la pomme n'a pas précisé si cette absence relevait d'une incompatibilité matérielle ou s'il s'agissait d'une une simple omission dans la liste des appareils pris en charge.
Une fonction dont l’absence reste inexpliquée
Reste désormais à savoir pourquoi les deux nouvelles montres ne figurent pas dans la liste des appareils compatibles. Comme nous venons de l'évoquer, Apple n’a donné aucune explication sur ce point, et rien ne permet pour l’instant d’affirmer que les Series 12 et Ultra 4 sont techniquement incapables de gérer la détection du lavage des mains. Pour tout vous dire, cela serait d'ailleurs assez surprenant.
Une différence matérielle pourrait malgré tout expliquer cette absence, même s’il peut aussi simplement s’agir d’une omission dans la documentation. Les nouvelles générations inaugurent notamment une nouvelle puce, avec plusieurs fonctions inédites liées à l’audio et à l’intelligence artificielle. En l'état, aucun élément ne permet cependant de relier ces changements à l’absence de la fonction sur les deux nouvelles montres.
Quoi qu'il en soit, pour les propriétaires des Series 11 et Ultra 3, rien ne change pour vous : la fonctionnalité reste prise en charge. Pour les Series 12 et Ultra 4, en revanche, le mystère reste entier quant à sa prise en charge.

articles.title: SEMICON India 2026 concludes with 15 announcements, headlined by Indian startups and student teams
articles.text:
SEMICON India 2026 concludes with 15 announcements, headlined by Indian startups and student teams
The final day put the spotlight on Indian startups and student teams building on homegrown chip platforms, alongside a new industry report projecting sharp growth for the country's semiconductor market.
New Delhi's Yashobhoomi convention centre wrapped up SEMICON India 2026 on September 19, 2026 with a concluding session that packed in 15 announcements, ranging from indigenous processor challenges to sovereign computing partnerships and skilling tie-ups, according to a press release from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
The day put the spotlight on Indian startups and student teams building on homegrown chip platforms, alongside a new industry report projecting sharp growth for the country's semiconductor market.
SEMICON India 2026, the fifth edition of the event, ran from September 17 to 19 and was jointly organised by the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) and SEMI on the theme 'Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem'.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the conference on its opening day. The event has grown into one of the country's largest semiconductor gatherings, bringing together government bodies, global chipmakers, academic institutions and start-ups as India works to build out design, manufacturing and packaging capabilities under its broader Semicon India programme.
Student teams turn indigenous chips into real products
The clearest entrepreneurial story from the closing session came from the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) Grand Challenge, organised by Maker Village under the Chips to Startup Programme of MeitY. The contest drew 1,236 teams comprising 5,045 participants, and three winning teams shared a total prize purse of Rs 60 lakh.
Meevisai Technologies, representing a SASTRA University team, took the first prize for an autonomous water-surface cleaning robot built on the indigenous SHAKTI processor developed by IIT Madras, aimed at cleaning ponds and temple tanks. Digiscope LLP won the second prize for VEGA Chikitsa, a digital stethoscope that captures heart and lung sounds with real-time filtering and machine-learning-assisted murmur screening, built on CDAC's VEGA processor. Zetawave Technologies, an IISc Bengaluru team, took the third prize for a forest-environment monitoring system, also on the VEGA platform.
Startups get investor time, and the market outlook brightens
Startup engagement ran through several other parts of the day. Under Startup Mitra, 11 startups pitched to more than 20 venture capital investors, with Elphins Technologies placing first, Meukron Technologies second, and Multi Nano Sense Technologies and CraftifAI sharing third place. A parallel SEMICON India Hackathon drew 3,808 team registrations from 881 colleges and 1,053 ideas, with 10 teams reaching the grand finale; teams from VIT Vellore and IIT Madras emerged as winners.
Adding context to the day's numbers, EY and the India Semiconductor and Electronics Association launched a report titled 'Semicon India 2.0: From Capacity Creation to Ecosystem Leadership'. The report estimates that India's semiconductor market could grow from nearly $64 billion in 2026 to $200 billion by 2035, and it lays out a roadmap for converting domestic demand and design talent into leadership across manufacturing, advanced packaging and innovation, reports suggest. Beyond the startup track, the session also saw C-DAC launch PARAM Vidya, a plug-and-play AI lab-in-a-box for universities and MSMEs, and PARAM Shavak-QS, a compact quantum simulation platform, alongside partnerships between C-DAC and NLC India, and C-DAC and Bharat Electronics Limited, for sovereign data-centre and computing infrastructure.
What is RISC-V and why India is betting on it
RISC-V is an open, royalty-free processor architecture, meaning any company or research group can design chips on it without paying licensing fees to a proprietary chip-design firm. For India, which has historically depended on foreign architectures for processor design, this matters because it lowers the barrier for home-grown players to build their own chips from the ground up.
That is why platforms like SHAKTI, developed at IIT Madras, and VEGA, developed by CDAC, carry weight beyond the prize money at events such as the DIR-V Grand Challenge. Each winning product built on these processors becomes a small proof point that Indian teams can design and deploy usable hardware on domestically developed silicon, rather than only assembling around imported chips.
Taken together, the concluding session's announcements, layered on top of 41 MoUs and initiatives unveiled during the first two days, point to an event that MeitY is positioning as a bridge between policy intent and on-ground execution. With the EY-ISEA report setting a 2035 horizon for India's semiconductor ambitions, the next test will be whether winning startups such as Meevisai and Digiscope, and the skilling partnerships announced alongside them, can scale from hackathon prototypes and MoUs into deployable products and a trained workforce over the coming years.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s latest Boring Company pitch involves a Hyperloop between Austin and San Antonio | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk recently claimed that his tunneling startup The Boring Company is working on “a simple precursor Hyperloop” between Austin and San Antonio that will reduce the journey between the two cities to less than 30 minutes.
The Boring Company account shared Musk’s statement and said it “would be excited and honored to build this massive infrastructure project.”
Many of The Boring Company’s announced projects — including tunnel systems in Chicago, Los Angeles, and between New York City and Washington, D.C. — have not materialized. However, it does operate a transportation system combining tunnels and surface routes in Las Vegas, and it recently raised a $3 billion round led by the United Arab Emirates.
Musk’s comments about a potential Austin-San Antonio Hyperloop were actually in reply to an AI-generated video depicting a generic science fiction future with human colonies on other worlds. Musk re-posted the video and declared, “This is the future we shall bring into being”.
Musk’s critics have argued that his vision of the future is apparently inspired by pulp science fiction and comic books; historian Jill Lepore recently told me that he seems to favor sci-fi that “completely defeats and defies all of his political beliefs.”

articles.title: Hacer turismo en un país y terminar visitando sus supermercados: la extraña fascinación de explorar otras cadenas
articles.text:
En 2024 las autoridades de Fujikawaguchiko, un pueblo de Yamanashi, Japón, tuvieron que hacer algo muy poco común: tapar sus mejores vistas al Fuji. Si te situabas en una calle concreta podías obtener una panorámica fascinante de su cumbre nevada, lo que hizo que decenas de miles de turistas se agolparan en la zona, entorpeciendo el tráfico, ensuciándolo todo y encaramándose a tejados. De ahí que decidieran construir una pantalla que impidiera las fotos. Lo más curioso es que los turistas no solo buscaban el Fuji. Les gustaba ese lugar en concreto porque podían retratar la montaña con una tienda Lawson en primer plano.
Quizás parezca anecdótico, pero conecta con un fenómeno cada vez más extendido en el sector: el turismo de supermercado o supermarket safaris.
¿"Turismo de supermercados"? Exacto. El término no lo hemos inventado nosotros. Lleva ya algún tiempo en el radar de los analistas dedicados a estudiar las tendencias del turismo mundial, como Booking, Skyscanner, la plataforma de turismo de la UE o el medio especializado Condé Nast Traveler, que en enero ya avanzaba que se trataría de una de las modas más relevantes de 2026.
Si buscas en TikTok te encontrarás también con un buen (buen) puñado de vídeos que tratan precisamente de eso: turistas recorriendo tiendas de países extranjeros y que comparten sus experiencias como quien visita un museo, un parque nacional o una catedral. No son los únicos. Hace poco Dayna Camilleri-Clarke, reportera especializada en viajes, publicó una crónica en la web de la CNN en la que reconoce su debilidad por los súper y ultramarinos extranjeros.
¿Tan relevante es? Sí. A finales de 2025 Hilton publicó un informe de tendencias turísticas en el que deslizaba dos datos interesantes. Primero, que el 48% de los viajeros cocina sus propias comidas durante sus vacaciones (algo que ha facilitado el éxito de los apartamentos turísticos). Segundo, que el 77% de los encuestados reconoce que disfruta del "turismo de supermercados".
Es decir, que más allá de que tengan que acudir a una tienda para comprarse pasta de dientes, un brick de leche, una barra de pan o cualquier otro producto que necesiten durante sus viajes, viven esas escapadas a las tiendas extranjeras como una experiencia turística en sí misma. No es obligación. Es devoción.
¿Hay más datos? Sí. Hilton no es el único que se ha dado cuenta de esa tendencia. Skyscanner asegura que el 35% de los turistas planea visitar o comprar en supermeracdos durante sus salidas al extranjero y que el 73% de los británicos acuden siempre o con frecuencia a tiendas locales cuando salen de su país.
De nuevo, la clave está en por qué dedicamos parte de nuestro tiempo a pasearnos entre estanterías con cajas de cereales, paquetes de pasta y conservas en vez de ir a la playa o visitar museos. Skyscanner descubrió que el 44% busca nuevos alimentos y bebidas, el 36% versiones locales de platos clásicos y el 33% marcas que no se veden en su propia ciudad. La plataforma de turismo de la UE incluso tiene un nombre para esa tendencia en auge: "safaris de supermercado".
"Los viajeros acuden en masa a los supermercados locales en busca de experiencias culturales auténticas. Impulsados por factores económicos y el atractivo de los encuentros genuinos, los súper se han convertido en los nuevos centros culturales", señala el organismo comunitario antes de recordar que ese 'boom' coincide con el encarecimiento de las entradas a monumentos y museos, lugares en los que además no es extraño encontrarse con largas colas.
 @jaja.ciao Ad @K-Supermarket | Are grocery stores the best form of tourism? I think so & Trip Advisor thinks so too 🙋 You don’t have to travel far for the best tourist destination in Finland, this one’s in just about every city 😍 you can get a taste of Finnish culture straight from the aisles of K-Supermarket. 🧡 My can’t-miss list for very Finnish specialties at a Finnish grocery store are: 1️⃣ BERRIES: enjoy berries in different forms: crushed berries, frozen berries, berry soup, berry juice, berry ice cream & fresh berries in summer 🫐 2️⃣ FRESH GOODIES: bakery items like iconic Finnish riisipiirakka & korvapuusti, Fresh fish that Finland’s known for, and fresh out the box pick & mix candies 🍬 3️⃣ LOCAL SPECIALTIES: if you’re in FInland, you have to try reindeer & salmiakki, so many variations to choose from. 🇫🇮 K-Supermarket is now a food destination, so next time you go shopping, slow down & embrace all the Finnish-ness around you 🛒
♬ original sound - Jade | Creator in Finland
¿Por qué nos gustan tanto? En su crónica Camilleri-Clarke desliza varias claves, pero pueden resumirse en una sola: cuando estamos en casa, en nuestra propia ciudad, las visitas al super suelen suponer tareas prácticas (vamos a un Mercadona, Dia, Eroski… porque necesitamos rellenar la nevera y la despensa), pero la cosa cambia si estamos en el extranjero, ya sea por ocio o por trabajo.
En esos casos los súper representan otra cosa, ventanas genuinas y auténticas al día a día del país que visitamos. Nos permite comprar pasta de dientes cuando se nos acaba, cierto, pero también descubrir nuevas marcas, comidas e ingredientes. No solo eso. Una visita a una tienda situada a miles de kilómetros de tu casa también puede revelarte nuevos formatos de packaging o reciclado.
¿Qué tienen de especial? Lo decíamos antes: los supermercados son espacios que nos permiten sumergirnos en el país que estamos visitando y conocer mejor su gastronomía y costumbres. Y con una ventaja extra: a menudo quedan fuera de los circuitos más turistificados. Lo que ocurrió con el Lawson de Fujikawaguchiko no es habitual. Lo normal es que las tiendas se queden fuera de los tours y no estén masificadas por turistas, con lo que conservan su carácter genuino.
Si eso no fuera suficiente, las tiendas ofrecen otros dos grandes atractivos. No importa si estás en un local de 7-Eleven de Osaka, un Walmart de Nueva York, un Tesco de Londres, un Pingo Doce de Oporto o un Mercadona de Barcelona, todos los supermercados se parecen entre sí y nos sentimos cómodos moviéndonos por sus pasillos. Son espacios familiares en los que podemos observar marcas, comidas e ingredientes nuevos que no se venden en nuestro país.
 @kendall.foerster4 Listen, grocery store tourism IS cultural immersion and I will not be taking questions at this time. 😂 One thing I’ve learned from living/traveling around Europe is just because two countries are neighbors does NOT mean their grocery stores carry all the same things. So when I’m in Italy, I stock up on the things I either can’t easily find back in Germany or that just hit different here. My current Italian grocery must-grabs: 🍋 Lemon soda - specifically the aggressively lemony kind 🧀 Cheese. Obviously. Whatever looks interesting goes in the cart. 🥩 Italian cured meats 🍝 Pasta shapes/brands I don’t normally see at home 🍅 Sauces, pestos & random jars 🍷 Wine because well… Italy And yes, I know I can find some Italian products in Germany. That’s not the point. The selection changes SO much once you cross a border in Europe, which is honestly one of my favorite little things about traveling here. Tell me - what am I missing? What should I add to my cart before I leave Italy? 👇🇮🇹
♬ Drop It Like It's Hot x Stayin Alive - NightBliz
¿Cuál es el otro atractivo? El precio. Visitar un super te permite disfrutar la comida local y sale más barato que ir a un restaurante o una cata. Y la experiencia no tiene por qué ser 'cutre'. Camilleri-Clarke reconoce que el mejor yogur que ha probado en su vida lo compró en una tienda de Atenas. Estaba plantada ante la nevera, ojeando etiquetas ininteligibles sin saber qué tarrina llevarse, cuando una señora estiró el brazo para llevarse un bote. Hizo lo mismo y aún lo agradece.
En los supermercados pueden comprarse también souvenirs. Por supuesto, Booking, Skyscanner y Hilton no son los únicos que se han dado cuenta. Ya hay cadenas de súper que han tomado nota del filón que tienen ante sí. La finlandesa K-Supermarket incluye algunas tiendas como atracciones turísticas en la web de Tripadvisor y la propia Mercadona ha comprobado cómo el peso de las compras de los visitantes ha ido creciendo a medida que lo hace el turismo español.

articles.title: Voyage pas cher : les erreurs qui font exploser le budget une fois sur place
articles.text:
Voyage pas cher : les erreurs qui font exploser le budget une fois sur place
Un vol à petit prix et un hôtel bien négocié ne suffisent pas à garantir des vacances économiques. Le budget commence souvent à déraper après l’arrivée, quand s’ajoutent le transfert depuis l’aéroport, les transports, les repas, les taxes locales, les retraits ou quelques gigaoctets consommés hors forfait. Pris séparément, ces montants paraissent parfois anecdotiques. Sur cinq ou sept nuits, ils peuvent pourtant effacer une bonne partie de l’économie réalisée au moment de réserver. Un voyage pas cher se prépare donc aussi pour ce qui se passe sur place, avec quelques vérifications simples et une marge pour les dépenses rarement mises en avant dans les offres.
Le budget peut déraper avant même la première visite
Une offre à 300 ou 400 euros par personne paraît parfois imbattable lorsqu’elle associe le vol et quelques nuits d’hôtel. Le problème vient souvent de ce qui n’est pas inclus : transfert, bagage, petit déjeuner, taxe locale ou trajets quotidiens.
Cette différence devient particulièrement visible lors d’un départ à la dernière minute. On compare facilement deux tarifs de séjour, beaucoup moins le coût réel d’une journée une fois arrivé à destination.
Choisir l’hôtel le moins cher sans regarder son emplacement
Une chambre moins chère à plusieurs kilomètres du centre de Barcelone, Rome ou Marrakech peut sembler être une bonne affaire. Elle le devient beaucoup moins lorsque deux personnes doivent prendre le métro, le bus ou un taxi plusieurs fois par jour.
La localisation doit donc entrer dans le calcul du prix. Une nuit à 90 euros près du cœur d’une ville peut finalement coûter moins cher qu’un hôtel à 70 euros mal desservi.
Même constat pour certains clubs en Espagne, en Grèce, en Tunisie ou au Maroc. Un établissement avec piscine et spa éloigné de tout convient parfaitement à des vacances reposantes. Pour un séjour consacré à la découverte, cette situation impose au contraire des déplacements supplémentaires.
Avant la réservation, mieux vaut regarder la distance réelle jusqu’aux activités prévues, les horaires des transports et le coût du retour en soirée.
Oublier le trajet entre l’aéroport et l’hébergement
Un billet d’avion très bas ne raconte pas toute l’histoire. Certains vols arrivent dans un aéroport situé à plusieurs dizaines de kilomètres de la destination affichée.
Une arrivée tardive peut également supprimer l’option du train ou du bus. Le taxi ou la navette privée devient alors presque obligatoire, avec une dépense imprévue dès la première heure du séjour.
La bonne comparaison consiste donc à additionner vol + bagages + transfert aéroport. Pour une famille, une course partagée peut rester raisonnable. Pour une personne seule partie avec un budget serré, elle pèse bien davantage.
Un vol légèrement plus cher mais arrivant dans un aéroport bien relié à la ville peut finalement être le meilleur choix.
Croire que le tarif de l’hôtel comprend tout
Petit déjeuner, parking, accès au spa, certaines activités ou même des équipements de l’établissement peuvent être facturés en supplément. Il faut aussi compter avec les taxes touristiques appliquées dans de nombreuses destinations.
En France, par exemple, leur montant dépend de la commune et du type d’hébergement. D’autres villes européennes utilisent également une taxation par personne et par nuit.
Sur un week-end, l'écart reste souvent limité. Sur un séjour d'une semaine pour plusieurs personnes, il mérite d'être intégré au budget avant le départ.
Le même raisonnement vaut pour les formules avec pension. Une offre tout compris peut sembler plus chère, mais devenir intéressante si l'hôtel se trouve dans une zone où chaque déjeuner et dîner devra autrement être payé au prix touristique.
Sous-estimer le budget repas
Un café, une glace, quelques bouteilles d'eau puis un dîner ne donnent pas forcément l'impression de beaucoup dépenser. C'est leur répétition qui fait la différence.
Dans une station balnéaire, sur certaines îles ou à proximité des monuments les plus fréquentés, les prix peuvent aussi grimper rapidement.
Il n'est pas nécessaire de consacrer ses vacances à comparer chaque addition. Quelques réflexes suffisent : éviter de prendre tous les repas dans les rues les plus touristiques, acheter l'eau et les encas dans un commerce local ou choisir un logement avec cuisine pour certains séjours longs.
Une formule avec petit déjeuner inclus peut également éviter une dépense quotidienne qui semblait insignifiante lors de la réservation.
Tout réserver à la dernière minute
Garder de la liberté est agréable. Découvrir sur place que la visite souhaitée n'est plus disponible qu'avec un billet premium l'est beaucoup moins.
Musées, excursions, parcs ou sorties en bateau affichent parfois des tarifs différents selon les créneaux et les canaux de réservation. Pour les activités incontournables, réserver en amont permet surtout de connaître la dépense.
L'erreur inverse consiste à remplir chaque journée d'activités payantes. Une promenade, une plage, un marché ou la découverte d'un quartier peuvent aussi occuper plusieurs heures sans faire bouger le budget.
| Dépense souvent oubliée | Impact possible | Réflexe utile | 
|---|---|---|
| Transfert aéroport | Moyen à élevé | Comparer bus, train, navette et taxi | 
| Hôtel éloigné | Élevé sur plusieurs nuits | Calculer les trajets quotidiens | 
| Petit déjeuner | Moyen | Vérifier s'il est inclus | 
| Taxe touristique | Faible à moyen | Regarder le tarif par pers. et par nuit | 
| Activités | Variable | Réserver les incontournables | 
| Repas | Élevé sur une semaine | Fixer une enveloppe quotidienne | 
Téléphone, paiements et petites dépenses : les frais qui passent sous le radar
Les coûts les plus frustrants sont souvent ceux qui n'améliorent en rien le voyage. Frais bancaires, mauvais taux de change ou données mobiles hors forfait peuvent représenter plusieurs dizaines d'euros dépensés sans contrepartie.
Ces postes sont pourtant parmi les plus faciles à anticiper avant de quitter la France.
Vérifier le roaming avant de passer la frontière
Dans l'Union européenne, l'itinérance permet généralement d'utiliser son forfait français dans des conditions proches de celles appliquées en France. Des limites sur la quantité de données peuvent néanmoins exister selon l'abonnement.
Le réflexe devient beaucoup plus important pour le Maroc, la Tunisie et d'autres destinations situées hors de la zone européenne. Quelques minutes de navigation ou l'utilisation intensive d'une application de cartographie peuvent alors être facturées séparément.
Le Royaume-Uni demande aussi une vérification. Certains opérateurs français continuent de l'inclure dans leurs offres, mais cette inclusion n'est plus imposée par le cadre européen.
Avant le départ, il suffit donc de regarder trois informations : pays inclus, enveloppe de données disponible et prix appliqué une fois cette limite dépassée.
Ubigi, Holafly ou GoMoWorld : une eSIM peut éviter le hors-forfait
Lorsque le forfait français couvre mal la destination, acheter une eSIMde voyage avant le départ peut revenir beaucoup moins cher que laisser fonctionner les données en itinérance.
Le principe est simple. Le voyageur conserve sa SIM principale pour son numéro habituel, mais utilise une seconde ligne numérique pour Internet. Encore faut-il disposer d'un smartphone compatible eSIM et régler correctement la ligne utilisée pour les données mobiles.
Ubigi propose des forfaits dans plus de 200 destinations, avec des offres nationales, régionales ou continentales. Une même eSIM peut être conservée et rechargée pour différents voyages, ce qui peut être pratique pour les personnes qui partent régulièrement à l'étranger.
Holafly mise davantage sur les gros consommateurs de data. Son catalogue couvre lui aussi plus de 200 destinations et de nombreuses offres sont proposées avec des données illimitées pendant une durée choisie. Il faut toutefois regarder les conditions de partage de connexion et les éventuelles politiques d'usage raisonnable selon le pays.
GoMoWorld adopte une logique plus simple autour de forfaits avec un volume défini. Le service annonce une couverture dans plus de 200 destinations et des plans à partir de 3,99 €, à installer puis à activer depuis son application au moment du voyage.
| eSIM | Positionnement | À regarder avant l'achat | 
|---|---|---|
| Ubigi | Forfaits pays et régionaux, eSIM réutilisable | Volume, durée et réseau local | 
| Holafly | Data importante, souvent illimitée | Hotspot et usage raisonnable | 
| GoMoWorld | Plans à volume défini dès 3,99 € | Nombre de Go et durée | 
Le moins cher n'est pas automatiquement le meilleur. Pour Google Maps, WhatsApp et quelques recherches, quelques gigaoctets peuvent suffire. Pour du télétravail, du streaming ou un partage de connexion avec un ordinateur, les besoins changent complètement.
Une précaution évite aussi une mauvaise surprise : après activation de l'eSIM, il faut vérifier que l'itinérance des données reste désactivée sur la SIM française si le forfait national n'inclut pas la destination.
Accepter automatiquement un paiement en euros
En dehors de la zone euro, certains terminaux et distributeurs proposent de convertir immédiatement le montant en euros.
Voir une devise connue semble rassurant. Le taux utilisé n'est pourtant pas toujours intéressant. Cette conversion dynamique peut inclure une marge supplémentaire par rapport au paiement dans la monnaie locale.
Mieux vaut donc connaître les frais appliqués par sa carte bancaire avant le voyage. Si la banque facture peu ou pas de conversion, payer dans la devise du pays est souvent plus avantageux.
Le même principe vaut au distributeur. Refuser une conversion proposée par la machine ne signifie pas refuser le retrait : la conversion sera simplement réalisée par l'établissement bancaire selon ses propres conditions.
Multiplier les petits retraits
Retirer une petite somme chaque jour paraît prudent. Lorsque chaque opération entraîne des frais fixes, cette habitude coûte rapidement plus cher qu'un nombre limité de retraits.
Certains distributeurs ajoutent également leur propre commission. Celle-ci doit être regardée avant de confirmer l'opération.
Dans une destination où la carte est largement acceptée, limiter les retraits simplifie donc le budget. Là où les espèces restent indispensables, mieux vaut retirer une somme raisonnable en une ou deux fois plutôt que multiplier les passages au distributeur.
Garder une seconde carte séparée de la première reste par ailleurs une précaution utile. Elle ne fait pas économiser d'argent directement, mais évite qu'un portefeuille perdu transforme un incident en urgence coûteuse.
Se fier uniquement au prix affiché par le comparateur
Un séjour à Marrakech à 450 euros peut finir plus cher qu'une offre à 520 euros si le premier exige de payer le transfert, le petit déjeuner et plusieurs trajets chaque jour.
Même logique pour un vol au départ de Paris à une heure très matinale. Le billet est peut-être moins cher, mais un taxi jusqu'à l'aéroport ou une nuit supplémentaire annule rapidement l'écart.
Comparer les voyages uniquement sur le tarif affiché revient donc à comparer des produits qui ne contiennent pas toujours la même chose.
Le chiffre utile reste le coût total prévisible du séjour : transport, hôtel, repas, connexion mobile et activités comprises.
Conserver une marge pour les imprévus
Même avec une bonne préparation, tout ne peut pas être prévu. Un bus raté, une météo capricieuse, une activité décidée sur place ou un restaurant plus cher que prévu font partie du voyage.
Le problème commence lorsque chaque euro du budget est déjà affecté avant le départ.
Garder environ 10 à 15 % de marge permet d'absorber ces dépenses sans passer le reste des vacances à recalculer chaque achat. Ce coussin n'a rien d'une règle absolue, mais il donne une vision plus réaliste du coût du séjour.
Un voyage économique ne consiste d'ailleurs pas à choisir systématiquement l'option la moins chère. L'objectif est plutôt d'éviter les dépenses qui n'apportent rien : data hors forfait, mauvais taux de change, hôtel trop éloigné ou transfert mal anticipé.
C'est souvent là que se joue la différence entre une véritable bonne affaire et un séjour qui paraissait seulement bon marché sur l'écran de réservation.

articles.title: Surfshark One : le VPN s’enrichit d’un antivirus à prix réduit
articles.text:
Déjà abonné au VPN ? Surfshark pousse l’antivirus comme complément logique
Surfshark propose une protection antivirus intégrée à son offre One, avec VPN, Alert, Search et Alternative ID, à partir de 2,79 € par mois avec la promotion actuelle.
Une protection antivirus qui complète le VPN
Si vous utilisez déjà Surfshark VPN, Surfshark One permet d’ajouter une protection antivirus et plusieurs outils de sécurité dans la même application. L’offre est actuellement proposée avec 85 % de réduction et jusqu’à 3 mois offerts, à partir de 2,79 € par mois sur la formule mise en avant.
Un VPN et un antivirus ne jouent pas exactement le même rôle. Le premier protège notamment la connexion et masque l’adresse IP, tandis que l’antivirus intervient directement sur les fichiers et programmes utilisés sur l’appareil.
Surfshark One réunit ces deux fonctions dans un même abonnement. Surfshark Antivirus analyse les fichiers pendant leur téléchargement, leur installation ou leur utilisation, avec une protection également prévue pour la webcam.
Le service affiche par ailleurs des résultats favorables aux tests d’AV-Test : 6/6 en protection, 5,5/6 en performances et 6/6 en convivialité. Un point intéressant pour ceux qui souhaitent renforcer la sécurité sans multiplier les logiciels installés.
| Fonction | Surfshark One | 
|---|---|
| VPN | Oui | 
| Antivirus | Oui | 
| Protection webcam | Oui | 
| Alertes de fuite de données | Oui | 
| Moteur de recherche privé | Oui | 
| Alternative ID | Oui | 
| Appareils | Illimités | 
| Garantie | 30 jours | 
L'offre ne s'arrête donc pas à l'antivirus. Surfshark Alert prévient notamment en cas de fuite concernant certaines données personnelles, tandis que Surfshark Search propose des recherches sans publicité ni traqueurs. Alternative ID permet de créer une identité et une adresse e-mail alternatives pour certains usages en ligne.
De mon côté, c’est surtout la simplicité qui retient mon attention avec Surfshark One. L’idée de retrouver le VPN, l’antivirus et les outils de protection dans une seule application évite de multiplier les logiciels. C’est un détail assez pratique au quotidien, notamment lorsqu’il faut rapidement vérifier un fichier ou consulter l’état de ses protections.
Surfshark One : une formule plus large que l’antivirus
Pour quelqu’un qui possède déjà Surfshark VPN, l’intérêt de l’offre dépend surtout des fonctions recherchées. Si l’objectif est uniquement d’ajouter un antivirus, une solution dédiée peut suffire. En revanche, One devient plus cohérent lorsqu’il faut également surveiller les fuites de données, limiter le pistage ou utiliser une identité en ligne alternative.
La promotion actuelle ramène le prix à 2,79 € par mois, contre un ancien tarif affiché de 7,12 € par mois, avec jusqu’à trois mois supplémentaires offerts. L’abonnement bénéficie aussi d’une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours.
Au final, Surfshark One ressemble davantage à un pack de sécurité complet qu’à un simple antivirus ajouté au VPN. Pour les utilisateurs déjà équipés de Surfshark, c’est surtout la possibilité de regrouper plusieurs protections dans une seule application qui mérite d’être comparée avant de souscrire.
